post.text:
AI is helping mathematicians make real progress on Navier-Stokes. A problem that has resisted humans for generations.

Super cool. But that’s not how a billion people are going to decide if AI matters.

They’re going to decide it matters when it gives them time back. When Sunday night isn’t spent doing expense reports. When a five-step approval becomes one step. When a doctor catches a disease earlier. When a kid anywhere in the world gets access to a great teacher. When healthcare gets better and more affordable.

Kevin Scott put it this way:
“A.I. is one of the most powerful things humans have ever invented for improving the quality of life of everyone, but it will take time. It should take time. We've always tackled super-challenging problems through technology. And so, we can either tell ourselves a good story about the future or a bad story about the future, and, whichever one we choose, that's probably the one that'll come true.”

The question is what we choose to do with it.

I think the best companies start with a vision: What is the world we want this technology to help create?

Then work backwards... Build toward that vision AND put the safeguards in place to do it responsibly.

The answer isn’t to start from fear, or to ignore the risks. It’s to be clear about the future we want, and build toward it with safeguards from the start.

This is a time for real leadership. Technical brilliance matters enormously. But so do judgment, experience, empathy, and an understanding of how businesses and institutions actually work, and how change actually lands on people.

The technology isn’t going to decide what kind of future we build with it. We will.

comments.comment:
Yes it’s true AI will help navigate the most difficult math equation but that’s not how common people will see the impact. From a workplace perspective AI can be most helpful if instead of excelling in repetitive tasks it has real impact to understand human interactions their quirks and risk tolerance. Under high pressure who will take advantage of risks and will it be benefiting us or extremely damaging for the company? If AI can test the real skills vs marketing self, one delivering results with no recognition? With new hire at C-suite shareholders and employees have great expectations can AI seriously assess who handled the toughest job risking their lifetime commitment, career prospects? 

AI needs to be a teacher that understands every student is different and match them to their strengths to master competency. 

Can AI help doctors identify problems just reading their notes without ordering extravagant costly tests? They will be AI fan where it alerts to see signs that the patient is lying as it questions their own ability, actions, decisions and hardwired habits? Scenario- Doctor asks patients-sleeping pills, pain killers and antidepressants based on personal childhood trauma? Can AI help in treating malignant drama?

author.name: Saran Vilvam
author.headline: “Empowering the Future of Business | LinkedIn Top Voice in Entrepreneurship 2024 | Founder & Chief executive officer of Zuave Sparkle Global Solutions | Building a Conglomerate | Innovating for a Better Tomorrow”

comments.comment: AI’s greatest opportunity is not simply to demonstrate what machines can achieve, but to create meaningful improvements in everyday human life. When innovation is guided by responsibility, empathy, and long-term vision, technology can expand access, save valuable time, and solve complex challenges at scale. The future depends on how thoughtfully we build it together.

author.name: Gabriel Rozo
author.headline: CFD Simulation for Oil & Gas, Petrochemical and Pharma | Simcenter STAR-CCM+ | Heat Exchangers, Cyclones, Furnaces, Reactors, Boilers, Evaporators, Compressors | Chemical Engineer, MSc Candidate FEQ/Unicamp | CAEXPERTS

comments.comment: Ryan Roslansky The opening is the part I'd gently push back on, not the claim, but treating it as the less useful half. I spent a few days inside the Lean formalisation of that proof rather than the announcement. What struck me wasn't the mathematics. It was that the result only counted because a verifier checked every logical step and refused to accept gaps: 2,486 files, nothing left open. Thousands of agents generated candidates; one mechanical checker decided which of them was a result rather than a plausible-looking draft. That is the piece that transfers to your list. Expense reports, five-step approvals, a doctor catching something earlier each of those is an output somebody has to trust before it gives anyone time back. Mathematics is unusual in having a verifier that is cheap, automatic and absolute. For almost everything on your list, that layer doesn't exist yet. So the vision question may have a companion worth asking alongside it: not only what world we want this to help create, but what plays the role of Lean in each of those domains. I suspect that's what the safeguards you mention actually look like in practice.

author.name: Johnny C. Taylor, Jr., SHRM-SCP
author.headline: President & CEO, SHRM | F500 Board Director | I help shape the future of work. Follow for expert insights on leadership, civility, and workforce growth.

comments.comment: Ryan, this is where human intelligence becomes the advantage rather than the afterthought. AI hands people an answer, and judgment is what turns it into a good decision. Companies investing in both will get far more out of the technology than the ones betting on the tools alone.

I agree. Breakthroughs on problems like Navier-Stokes show how far AI’s capabilities are advancing, but everyday usefulness will determine its impact at scale. The real measure will be how much time, access, and capability it gives back to people.

author.name: Yandong Xiao
author.headline: Senior Backend Software Engineer | Solving Scale, Reliability, and Deployment Bottlenecks Across Distributed Cloud and AI Platforms

comments.comment: The breakthroughs are exciting, but most people will probably judge AI by whether a frustrating workflow suddenly becomes easier. Those small everyday wins are often what make a technology feel real.

author.name: Rafi Seddiqi
author.headline: Weaver.Work + Laoh.Work | Built from Axioms. Proven with Math

comments.comment:
I think the critical question is: who is “we”? Are we asking people what they want to do with AI, or are we asking ourselves and answering the question on their behalf?

We should not ignore the fact that people with big egos are potentially deciding the future of AI, already. This means your notion of empathetic leaders is an absolute requirement for the future of humanity, not just AI.

An empathetic leader will not only ask, but also listen.

author.name: Chuck Shaver
author.headline: Founder, CS Sales Consulting | Building LinkedIn Social Selling Programs for B2B Sales & Marketing Leaders | Market Research + Sales Tech + Strategy & Execution | Stay Top of Mind. Build Pipeline. Close Deals Faster.

comments.comment:
This is the part of the AI conversation that matters most.  The breakthrough won’t be when people are impressed by what AI can do. It will be when they stop thinking about AI altogether because it quietly removed friction from their day.  Less admin. Faster decisions. Better healthcare. More personalized education. More time spent on work and people that actually matter.

I've cut my processes by 80% with AI and rebuilt my entire website in 2 hours yesterday.

author.name: Xavier Elletson
author.headline: Founder & CEO, Unstuck LLC | AI-Driven Biomimetic Engineering & High-Efficiency Infrastructure IP | Performance-Based Overhead Reduction | Replacing Paid Cloud Software & Manual Admin Labor with Local Offline AI Systems

comments.comment: Perfect perspective. Technical breakthroughs in pure mathematics show the incredible capability of frontier models, but societal adoption is built on human utility. For enterprises and leaders, the true ROI of AI isn't raw benchmark scores it's giving people time back, eliminating administrative drag, and empowering teams to focus on high value judgment.
